title: Handbook: Inventory
publisher: KPMG LLP, U.S. Department of Professional Practice
source_classification: October 2025 U.S. GAAP interpretive handbook reproducing ASC 330 excerpts; professional guidance, not the authoritative Codification itself or proof of the latest edition
questions: How are variable and fixed production overhead assigned to inventory at normal, abnormally low, and abnormally high output?
When are idle capacity, abnormal waste, and standard costs reflected in inventory or current expense?
inspected_summary: KPMG explains that variable production overhead follows actual facility use while fixed production overhead is allocated over an entity-specific normal-capacity range that considers expected variation and planned maintenance. When production is abnormally low, unit fixed overhead is not increased and the unallocated amount is expensed; at abnormally high production, the per-unit allocation is reduced so inventory is not carried above cost. Its example uses $700,000 monthly fixed overhead and 1,000 normal tons: at 600 tons, $420,000 is included in inventory and $280,000 expensed; at 2,000 tons, $350 per ton is allocated. It says idle-plant overhead, unanticipated spoilage and abnormal freight/handling are period costs, while inherent anticipated spoilage is included in production cost. It also reproduces ASC 330-10-30-12: standard costs are acceptable only when adjusted at reasonable intervals to reasonably approximate a recognized cost basis at the balance-sheet date.

title: Standard Costing and ABC: A Coexistence
publisher: Institute of Management Accountants, Strategic Finance magazine
jurisdictions: United States; professional practice, not law
source_classification: Professional practitioner magazine article; conceptual and nonauthoritative
questions: When can activity-based drivers improve decision-cost information over broad volume allocations?
How can standard-cost systems and activity-based analysis be combined?
How should allocated costs be interpreted in product or service profitability?
inspected_summary: The article explains that broad volume-based overhead allocation can distort product, service, or customer profitability when resource consumption differs. Activity-based costing groups resource costs into activity pools and applies causal consumption drivers to cost objects; standard costing can coexist with ABC analysis, and the article discusses incremental or marginal costs for decisions. These are management-costing principles, not a required allocation rule for external reporting. The article also distinguishes decision information from the inventory cost basis used for external reporting.

title: Handbook: Revenue recognition
publisher: KPMG LLP, U.S. Department of Professional Practice
entity_roles: contractors and other vendors reporting customer contracts
source_classification: December 2025 U.S. GAAP interpretive handbook reproducing ASC 606 excerpts and implementation examples; professional guidance, not the authoritative Codification itself or proof of the latest edition
questions: How does a job-cost measure of progress differ from allowable-cost billing and incurred-cost settlement?
How do contract assets, receivables and contract liabilities relate to performance and billing?
When can an over-time service contract be shown as WIP versus a contract asset or receivable?
When may variable consideration associated with a customer contract enter the Topic 606 transaction price, and what happens when that estimate changes?
How does a change in transaction price affect revenue already recognized for satisfied or partially satisfied performance obligations?
inspected_summary: KPMG's ASC 606 Example 19 describes a $5.0 million building refurbishment contract with $4.0 million expected costs, including $1.5 million of procured elevators. Because elevator cost would overstate progress, the contractor excludes it from the cost-to-cost measure and recognizes the elevator transfer at zero margin. With $0.5 million of other cost incurred against $2.5 million remaining measured costs, progress is 20 percent: $0.7 million revenue on adjusted transaction price plus $1.5 million elevator revenue, $2.2 million total revenue, and $2.0 million cost. KPMG also explains that contract assets/liabilities are presented net per contract, unconditional rights are receivables, and recognized performance before an unconditional right produces a contract asset; amounts received or due before performance produce a contract liability. The guide says over-time performance does not create a separate WIP asset when the customer controls the asset as it is created; the entity records a contract asset or receivable as revenue is recognized. These are financial-reporting principles, separate from FAR allowable-cost and billing rules. The December 2025 guide also explains that variable consideration is included only subject to the significant-reversal constraint and that a change allocated to a satisfied or partially satisfied performance obligation is recognized as revenue or a reduction in the period of change. It explicitly says invoicing does not determine whether the right to payment is unconditional; legal rights, contract terms, and the facts and circumstances control.

OEM incentives and floorplan debt
Dealer service, parts and rental revenue
OEM warranty work versus dealer-sold third-party protection

inspected_summary: Titan reports new/used equipment at lower of cost or net realizable value by specific identification; used trade-ins are initially valued using estimated resale price less expected gross profit and reconditioning, with later NRV review; reconditioning/preparation costs are WIP. Parts use lower of average cost or NRV. Inventory purchase incentives reduce inventory and cost of revenue when the unit sells, while qualifying expense reimbursements reduce related expense when earned. Service plus consumed parts are recognized over time using the amount Titan has the right to invoice for labor and parts, with unbilled receivables moved to receivables when invoiced; standalone parts sales are point-in-time. Short-term rental revenue is straight-line; advance or arrears billings create deferred rental revenue or unbilled receivables. Dedicated rental fleet is depreciated PP&E while some equipment inventory can also be rented; contract types and rent-to-purchase options affect classification and cash flow evidence. Manufacturer floorplan balances/cash flows are distinguished from nonmanufacturer financing; Titan's financials describe specific CNH, bank and DLL terms, collateral, interest-free/reduced-rate periods and sales/rental-linked repayment. OEMs provide new-equipment/parts warranties, reimburse Titan for repairs, and may offer extended warranties; Titan also offers third-party protection for some used units. All are issuer-specific policies and contract arrangements.

title: Florida Statutes § 718.111, Association Powers and Duties
source_classification: Official state condominium statute; legally binding only for its scope in Florida, not an accounting standard
questions: What association accounting records and source documents must be maintained?
What GAAP preparation, compilation, review, audit and cash-reporting thresholds apply?
How are reserve and operating cash legally segregated or accounted for?
inspected_summary: The 2026 statute requires detailed receipts/expenditures, bank statements and ledgers, source invoices/receipts/deposit slips, unit assessment ledgers and financial reporting records. It requires complete GAAP financial statements when the statutory criteria apply: revenues of $150,000-$299,999 compiled; $300,000-$499,999 reviewed; $500,000 or more audited; under $150,000 a cash-receipts-and-expenditures report, with member-vote alternatives subject to statutory limits. Reserve cash may be commingled with operating funds only for investment, must be separately accounted for, and the commingled balance cannot fall below the reserve amount. The rule concerns statutory records, reporting thresholds and fund control; it does not settle financial-statement presentation of reserve assessments.

title: Florida Statutes § 718.112, Bylaws and Reserve Requirements
source_classification: Official state condominium statute; legal reserve and voting controls, not financial-statement recognition authority
questions: What reserve-study funding and special-assessment restrictions apply in Florida condominiums?
What notice and voting conditions apply to selected nonemergency special assessments and reserve uses?
How do statutory reserve studies relate to annual reports and reserve disclosures?
inspected_summary: The statute requires reserve calculations using useful life, replacement cost/deferred maintenance and, for associations within the structural-integrity-study provisions, the study's recommendations for specified components. It describes member authority to vote on underfunding subject to SIRS exceptions, identifies special assessments/credit/loans as possible funding tools for covered structural items with a majority vote of total voting interests, and restricts developer-controlled associations from reserve waivers/reductions before turnover. Reserve funds generally stay in reserve accounts and other uses require advance vote, with a stricter rule for applicable SIRS components. Nonemergency special-assessment meetings require 14-day notice. These are specific legal powers/controls and do not decide when assessment income is recognized under GAAP or whether the future project is capitalized.

inspected_summary: Upon turnover, a developer must deliver association property under its control, including financial records and source documents from incorporation through turnover.
